summary: Describes experiments involving over 100,000 hosts to evaluate the availability, accuracy, and reliability of time distribution using the Network Time Protocol across the Internet.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1128 reports experiments testing how widely available and accurate Internet time service was, with a focus on NTP. The results show that NTP could usually keep time within a few tens of milliseconds across much of the Internet, while also documenting sources of error.

subtitle: Experiments measuring the availability and accuracy of Internet time service using NTP.

tldr.problem: Internet paths, hosts, and radio clocks introduce delays and failures that can make it difficult to distribute accurate time.
tldr.mechanism: The paper surveys time-serving hosts and measures NTP offsets and delays across Internet paths and radio synchronization sources.
tldr.outcome: The experiments report that time at most parts of the Internet could ordinarily be kept within a few tens of milliseconds, even during some failures or disruptions.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 1128's status as Unknown. The RFC says that it reports experiments and does not specify a standard.

sections.title: Testing Internet Time Distribution
sections.content:
This paper reports experiments on the availability, accuracy, and reliability of time distribution over the Internet. It surveys hosts and gateways using three time protocols, then studies NTP measurements along selected network paths and radio synchronization paths.

The paper does not define NTP's architecture or protocol in detail. It evaluates the results of time requests and measurements collected during the experiments described in the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC measures how many hosts answered time requests and how accurate their clocks appeared. It focuses on observed results, not on defining the NTP protocol.

sections.title: How NTP Estimates Clock Differences
sections.content:
NTP servers exchange timestamps so peers can estimate round-trip delay and the clock offset between them. The paper explains that the estimates are filtered to reduce noise, then used to select a peer and adjust the host clock's phase and frequency.

Primary servers synchronize to external sources such as radio clocks; secondary servers synchronize to primary servers and other configured peers. Multiple servers and paths help the synchronization subnet continue operating when connectivity or a time source is disrupted.
sections.plainLanguage: NTP compares timestamps sent in both directions to estimate how far clocks differ. It filters those measurements and uses selected peers to adjust a computer's clock.

sections.title: Survey Results and Sources of Error
sections.content:
A survey attempted to read clocks at 107,799 distinct host addresses. Of these, 20,758 returned an apparently valid indication in at least one protocol; the RFC cautions that these counts describe the survey and its selection process.

For carefully measured NTP paths, the filtered sample results showed a median error of a few milliseconds and a maximum error no more than 50 milliseconds. The paper also identifies network delay variation, radio propagation, and radio-clock behavior as sources that can limit accuracy.
sections.plainLanguage: Some surveyed systems returned accurate time, while others had large errors or did not answer. Filtering improved measurements on the NTP paths examined, but network and radio delays still mattered.

sections.title: What the Experiments Suggest
sections.content:
The paper concludes that NTP can provide useful timekeeping across a statistically variable Internet, while noting limits from radio clocks, local clock hardware, network paths, and implementation quality. Its abstract says time throughout most portions of the Internet could ordinarily be maintained within a few tens of milliseconds, including some cases of disruption.

The author identifies possible improvements to radio-clock designs, timebase hardware, frequency estimation, and monitoring. The document reports measurements and suggestions rather than establishing a new standard.
sections.plainLanguage: The measurements show that Internet time service can be accurate, but its quality depends on clocks, radio signals, and network paths. The paper suggests improvements rather than defining a new protocol.
